$comment: Every shell the app knows how to launch, on every platform, in one place.
Read by src/main/shells.ts and src-tauri/src/shells.rs. It exists because
those two files previously held the same table twice, in two languages, and
adding macOS and Linux would have made that six copies. A new shell is an
`candidates` are tried in order and the first that exists on disk wins, so a
shell installed by Homebrew on Apple silicon, Homebrew on Intel, and the
system is one entry rather than three. ${VAR} is expanded from the
environment; a candidate whose variable is unset is skipped rather than
producing a path with a hole in it.
`integration` names a launch mechanism, not a script. The three are
genuinely different pieces of engineering — a command-line flag, an rc file
argument, and an environment variable pointing at a directory — so each host
implements the three and this file only says which applies.

pwsh-candidates: Listed for all three platforms because PowerShell 7 is genuinely
cross-platform and someone who chose it on Windows will want it on a Mac.
The homebrew paths come before /usr/bin so a user-installed 7.x wins over
bash-order: Homebrew first, and this one matters on macOS: /bin/bash is bash 3.2 from
2007, kept at that version for licensing reasons. The integration script
uses PROMPT_COMMAND as an array on 5.1+, and 3.2 takes the string path —
it works either way, but anyone who installed a modern bash meant it.
fish: No integration: fish is not POSIX and posix.sh would not parse in it. It
launches and works, minus folder tracking and command-finished alerts —
the same deal cmd.exe and WSL already get. A fish port of the script is a
third file, and that is a trade to make when someone actually wants it.
ssh: On all three platforms, and that is not a compromise: Windows has
shipped OpenSSH since 10/1809, at the System32 path listed above. So an
SSH pane is the same feature everywhere, unlike WSL.
`integration: none`, and this is the honest part. The integration script
lives on *this* machine; the shell answering on the far end has never
seen it and emits nothing. So an SSH pane has no folder tracking and no
command-finished alerts — the same deal cmd.exe, WSL and fish get. What
still works is everything read off the byte stream: activity detection,
the bell, and an agent's own declared state via `iaw`.
Making it work would mean writing a file onto someone else's machine,
which is a decision for the person whose machine it is, not a default.
No `login: true` either: the login shell is requested inside the remote
command instead, because -l here would be handed to ssh rather than to
login: POSIX shells launch as login shells because that is where a Mac's PATH
comes from: /etc/zprofile runs path_helper, and a non-login shell skips
it, leaving panes without /usr/local/bin. Windows has no equivalent, so
